newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Managing the economy with a GST.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Managing the economy with a GST.

text.p: A goods and services tax (GST) could represent much more than rationalisation of the Australian tax system; it might also be a better tool for demand management, which is currently the domain of monetary policy.
There are at least three strong advantages in manipulating the economy with a consumption tax instead of interest rates:
--The tax would probably be faster-acting.
--A policy tightening would not strangle investment.
--It would not encourage currency gyrations.
The most attractive prospect is the immediacy of a change in direct tax rates.
If one left people with less cash in their pockets, then they could not spend so much. But if the economy were slow, giving them more money should quickly juice things up a bit.
Surely, too, any demand management tool that acted on consumption would maximise long-run economic potential, because businesses would not be squeezed out of investment.

"It should be faster acting because, rather than acting on investment, which stems from long-term decision-making, it would affect day-to-day consumption decisions," said Access Economics analyst Chris Richardson.
Imagine how much more useful a fast-acting shot of fiscal adrenalin would have been in July, when the Reserve Bank belatedly realised that the economy was too slow.
That boost would have already flowed through the economy's veins to suppress, or maybe reverse, the current rise in unemployment.
The bank might still have eased monetary policy, intending to wind back the fiscal boost a few months later when interest rates were expected to bite.

Even more strikingly, wouldn't a quick fiscal boost have been a great substitute for this month's rate cut, which will have little effect until well into 1997, far too late to do anything about the economy's current flatness.
How much easier it would be to manage inflation if one only had to look a few months ahead, knowing that a stimulus could be rapidly unwound.
The bank itself would wield the GST rate, subject to delivering some long-run average revenue target set by the government.
One imagines the bank effecting gentle monetary policy adjustments as a trimming device, leaving the sharp countercyclical manoeuvres to the GST rate.
Probably, the variable GST would be phased in to give the bank time to get a feel for it.
Would the bank want it? Yes, almost certainly it would appreciate monetary policy getting a little fiscal help.

Macquarie Bank senior economist John Kyiakopoulos said a variable GST might be inflationary unless unions, for example, were confident that rises would be followed by falls. Handing it to the Reserve Bank, with its independent credibility, might be an important element of the policy, he supposed.

Playing the devil's advocate, Kyriakopoulos also pointed to a GST being regressive, which would be exaggerated if it were jacked up to dampen demand. On the other hand, one notes that high interest rates can also hit low-income earners hardest.
This is not an original idea.
A variable GST was pushed a few years ago by, among others, Garry White, who is now executive director of Corporate Economics Australia, a consultancy.

White now thinks the government is better off not managing demand at all. But he still believes that if the authorities must meddle then a variable GST is the way to do it, partly because it would leave the currency alone.
"Exports would be unaffected, whereas if you tighten monetary policy you push up the exchange rate, which makes our exports less competitive," he said.

But note that the monetary effect on the exchange rate is not necessarily a bad thing. By raising the exchange rate during booms, it diverts demand into imports, which eases inflationary pressure at the most critical time.

A final point is that there seems to be no constitutional obstacle to letting an authority such as the bank set tax rates. Macquarie University law professor Tony Blackshield, a constitutional specialist, told Reuters he saw no problem with a tax rate being set administratively, rather than by law.
